note: VERIFIED BY ORCHA — the P1 differential metric is measuring the wrong thing. src/differential.zig groupByResult() keys boards by a hash of OUTPUT VALUES; compare() then labels the largest value-group 'agreements' and every other value-group a 'disagreement'. It never compares implementations to each other. 'area_score 2x2: 19/81, 6 disagreements' means 19 boards share the modal score and 7 distinct scores exist (19 + six other groups = 81). exp6.genericAreaScore and Rules(w,h).area_score are line-for-line identical INCLUDING their neighbour functions; they agree on all 81 and all 729 boards. Correct metric: per board, evaluate every impl, count boards where all results are equal; a disagreement is a board where they differ, reported with each impl's differing value. Your TDD fixture passed because it only asserted that more than one group appears — it cannot distinguish 'impls disagree' from 'outputs vary'. That is the broken-positive-control class already on record as CODE.M4A-HARNESS's A6 fixture: a control that passes for the wrong reason. Fix the metric, re-run, and treat the first matrix as not yet taken.

STANDING REQUIREMENT for every instrument this sprint builds or touches — red-green-refactor applied to the instruments themselves (Beck TDD; maxim: never trust a test you haven't seen fail). Before an instrument's first real reading is believed it must pass BOTH controls: (1) NULL CONTROL — give it the same implementation twice; it must report perfect agreement. Today's harness fails this instantly and nobody ran it. (2) SEEDED-DEFECT CONTROL — register a deliberately mutated copy of a real implementation (flip a comparison, change a constant, swap an argument); the instrument must report it as a disagreement, naming the witness inputs. A positive control alone is not enough: this harness's known-bad fixture passed for the wrong reason, because groupByResult produces multiple groups whenever OUTPUTS vary. Same defect class as CODE.M4A-HARNESS's A6 fixture. NOTE THE LEVERAGE: a mutant is just another implementation, so the differential harness IS a mutation-testing rig (DeMillo/Lipton/Sayward 1978) at no extra cost. Registering mutants as implementations gives a mutation score — the percentage of injected faults the comparison catches — which is a measured answer to 'can our checks ever go red'. Build it that way rather than as a one-off fix. SECOND ITEM: sort the duplicate implementations into CLONES and INDEPENDENTS before counting oracle value. exp6.genericAreaScore and Rules.area_score are line-for-line identical including neighbour functions — that is copy-paste, and clones cannot catch each other's errors. Only uncorrelated origins count as oracles: the Python reference, exp4 vs exp6 as different generations, the tested core vs the solvers. Report the two categories separately; agreement among clones is worth nothing and must not be reported as reassurance.
